title: The Tally of Dishonor — Editor Intro
summary: Editorial opening splash that re-arms the live pressures entering Issue 6 without recapping the prior issue or revealing later issue payoffs.
settingText: Ordinary neighborhood bank lobby and glass facade, morning
panelPlan: Full-page editorial/title splash using the bank's visual contradiction: large transparent glass, small desks, queue ropes, screens and ordinary customers, with no visible treasure anywhere.
Bjorn should read the room like a fortification that has forgotten to fortify anything. Carrie is already in service-mode; Gunnar studies the system rather than the security.
Use glass, blank walls and polished floor reflections for integrated caption typography. Give 'The hoard has an appointment desk.' a dry visual punch before the title.
Do not show the teller conversation, account result, card, household purchases, debt ledger, toaster, or later issue conclusions.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: Most hoards have the decency to exist somewhere.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: New York keeps its money as numbers behind glass.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: Bjorn would like to see the hoard.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: The hoard has an appointment desk.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: Welcome to THE TALLY OF DISHONOR.

directionInline.text: Non-diegetic opening editorial/title page. It must entice rather than recap. Preserve the exact caption text and integrate it as designed page typography, not speech balloons. Use full-page cinematic sequential-comic art in the established Vikings painted documentary-comedy language. The page may promise the issue's central pressure but must not reveal later solutions, reversals, or payoffs.

source: Season editorial intro/teaser pass developed September 30, 2026.

title: The Glass Place
summary: Carrie gets Bjorn and Gunnar to the bank because the provisional account/rent setup is still unresolved; the real pressure is that ordinary household needs still depend on money the Vikings cannot independently use.
settingText: Busy NYC sidewalk approaching the bank
panelPlan: Wide: Carrie moves fast down a crowded sidewalk with a DTI folder; Bjorn and Gunnar keep pace.
Medium: Bjorn carries the small wrapped hacksilver pouch he still considers real money.
Medium: Gunnar recognizes the same glass-fronted bank from an earlier walk and points it out ahead through the pedestrian traffic.
Close on Carrie: Still moving, she gives Gunnar a tired sideways look when he reminds her they have passed the same entrance before.
Wide at the bank entrance: The three stop beneath the ordinary branch signage and glass doors; Bjorn cuts off the sidewalk argument and directs everyone inside.

dialogueInline.text: Account setup is still open. No account, no rent setup. Housing keeps flagging it.
Then we get the account today.
Good. Then at least one of us is awake.

title: A Retail Fortress
summary: Bjorn's expectation of a defended treasury collides with an ordinary branch full of customers, while Carrie tries to keep the appointment socially normal.
settingText: Outside and inside ordinary bank branch
panelPlan: Wide: Ordinary glass-fronted bank branch with ATM vestibule, queue ropes and fluorescent lobby.
Medium: Gary, the security guard, helps an older customer with the ATM before noticing the trio.
Close: Bjorn studies Gary's knee brace and relaxed posture.
Medium: Gary looks down at the brace.
Wide: Carrie steers Bjorn toward the teller line.

dialogueInline.text: Do you guard the money with an injured knee?
Mostly people guard their own money.

title: The Teller
summary: Kevin begins the account as an ordinary service interaction, and Bjorn's age becomes briefly strange without turning the whole scene into spectacle.
panelPlan: Wide: Kevin receives the DTI identity packet across the teller desk.
Medium: He reaches the birth-date field and stops.
Medium: Carrie does not look up from her folder.

Close on Bjorn across the teller desk: He waits with grave patience while Kevin and Carrie puzzle over the birth year; Gunnar's comment about the building's age lands beside him without changing his expression.
Medium: Kevin decides not to engage and keeps processing.

dialogueInline.text: Government ID, tax substitute, address verification.
Was he born in eight seventy-nine?
I was hoping the first read was a typo.
He is older than this building.

title: Address Is a Place
summary: A proof-of-address requirement exposes the gap between actually living somewhere and being legible to a financial institution, but Carrie solves it without turning the whole issue into a paperwork campaign.
panelPlan: Medium: Kevin turns one screen toward Carrie.
Insert: Carrie places the DTI placement letter and provisional housing confirmation beside the screen.
Medium: Kevin points to the required document field rather than arguing.
Close: Gunnar looks from the letter to the teller window.
Medium: Carrie asks for the branch manager.

dialogueInline.text: I still need proof of address.
He sleeps there. DTI put him there. Here is the letter saying both of those things.
The system needs one document it recognizes.
We live there. The bank doesn't know yet.
How can the place be true to us and not true to the bank?
It isn't false. It isn't verified.
A document the bank already trusts.
Then teach the bank to trust this one.

title: Worthy Silver
summary: Bjorn offers hacksilver as a sincere opening deposit and learns that modern money can reject valuable metal while still accepting a number backed by institutional recognition.
panelPlan: Medium: Bjorn unwraps a small piece of hacksilver and places it carefully on the counter.
Close: Kevin looks at it without touching it.
Two-shot: Bjorn looks genuinely offended, not confused.
Medium: Gunnar turns the hacksilver in his fingers after Kevin slides it back.
Close on Carrie: She watches Gunnar turn the rejected hacksilver over in his fingers, then looks back at Bjorn as the distinction between value and accepted currency sinks in.

dialogueInline.text: We cannot deposit that as currency.
Yes. It is just not dollars.
It buys food where I come from.
Worth something. Just not to this room.
I dislike money that changes when I cross a street.

title: Carrie's Fifty
summary: Carrie supplies the minimum cash deposit, and Bjorn only accepts once the money is named as debt rather than charity.
panelPlan: Insert: Carrie places fifty dollars on the counter.
Medium: Kevin looks between the cash and Carrie.
Medium: Bjorn does not let Carrie answer for him.
Two-shot across the teller desk: Carrie holds Bjorn's gaze while reframing her fifty dollars as a debt he can repay; the cash remains physically between them on the counter.
Close on Bjorn: After a beat he gives one deliberate nod, accepting the money only once the obligation has a form he recognizes.

dialogueInline.text: Then don't. Owe me fifty. After rent and food.
Do you two want a minute?
No. This is how he says thank you.

title: The Account
summary: Henderson accepts the DTI housing record, opens the account, and gives Bjorn the debit card; the institutional problem is resolved by the end of the first act.
panelPlan: Wide: Henderson reviews the DTI placement letter and Kevin's screen at a small manager desk.
Medium: Carrie pushes the file back into order.
Insert: Kevin activates a blue debit card and slides it toward Bjorn.
Close on Bjorn: He turns the blue debit card over slowly, inspecting the blank plastic object that now stands between him and the recorded money.
Medium on Henderson: The manager explains the bank's guarantee in the same practical tone used for any customer while Bjorn and Gunnar listen across the desk.
Close on Bjorn and Carrie: Bjorn looks from the card to Carrie as he reduces the arrangement to a promise that can be spent; Carrie can see that this formulation actually works for him.

dialogueInline.text: This qualifies under the alternative-document policy.
So the money is a number.
And the card tells them which number is ours?
The bank records the balance and guarantees it.
Then your promise is what spends.

title: A Thing That Exists
summary: Because Bjorn distrusts an account that exists only as recorded value, Henderson gives him the branch's absurd promotional toaster, accidentally providing the tangible acknowledgment he wanted.
settingText: Bank manager desk and supply alcove
panelPlan: Medium: Bjorn puts the card down rather than pocketing it.
Medium: Henderson gestures toward a stack of new-account promotional boxes.
Insert: A plain metal toaster comes out of the box.
Close on Gunnar: He studies the plain metal toaster with genuine curiosity, tracing the two bread slots and lever as a tangible machine rather than a banking symbol.
Two-shot across the manager desk: Carrie looks at Henderson in disbelief while he calmly confirms the toaster promotion; the boxed appliance sits absurdly between the account paperwork.
Medium: Bjorn lifts the box with solemn approval.

dialogueInline.text: We do have the new-account promotion.
Does the bank give us a bread machine for keeping money here?
Do not ask follow-up questions. Take the toaster.
The number came with a toaster.
I swear this is not how banking works.

title: Outside With Too Much Iron
summary: The bank story ends; Bjorn immediately tries to settle Carrie's debt, and she forces him to think about money as household capacity rather than honor resolved in one gesture.
panelPlan: Wide: Bjorn exits carrying the toaster box under one arm, debit card in the other hand.
Medium: He offers the debit card to Carrie.
Two-shot: Bjorn does not lower his hand.
Close on Gunnar: He looks from the debit card to Bjorn's still-outstretched hand, thinking through how owing money and retaining spending money can both be true.
Medium on the sidewalk: Carrie points them toward home while Bjorn finally pockets the card, the toaster box tucked under his other arm.

dialogueInline.text: And you owe rent. And you need food. Keep the card.
Can you owe fifty and still spend fifty?
That is how men lose fifty.
That is also how people buy groceries.

title: What Is Needed
summary: The toaster arrives home as an odd object, but the real turn is the household making its first shared spending list and revealing separate practical wants.
panelPlan: Wide: Bjorn sets the boxed toaster on the table. Astrid and the two male Kin gather around while Gunnar removes the packaging.
Medium: Astrid examines the toaster slots, then points to a torn seam in her clothing.
Medium: First Male Kin lifts the nearly empty detergent sample from the DTI starter bag.
Medium: Second Male Kin points to the last piece of fruit from the bodega.
Wide: Carrie lays rent estimate and blank paper beside the toaster.
Close: Bjorn puts the debit card in the center of the table.

dialogueInline.text: Rent. Food. Laundry. Needles. One thing nobody needs.
Because if every dollar only fixes a problem, you're gonna hate money.

title: The Tally
summary: Gunnar turns the account into a finite household tally, and Bjorn sees that modern money is useful precisely because spending it forces choices among real obligations.
panelPlan: Insert: Gunnar writes simple categories with numbers: RENT, FOOD, SOAP, CARRIE 50.
Medium over the household tally: Bjorn plants one finger beside CARRIE 50, insisting on the personal debt while Gunnar's other categories remain visible around it.
Medium: Carrie moves the rent line above it.
Two-shot: Bjorn resists, then looks at the people around the table.
Close: Bjorn lets the rent line remain on top.

dialogueInline.text: If we pay her first and miss rent, we owe her fifty from a worse room.

title: Different Wants
summary: The household narrows the shopping trip together, preserving group continuity while making individual preference visible before anyone begins independent neighborhood routines.
panelPlan: Wide: Astrid, First Male Kin and Second Male Kin remain together at the table with the shopping list between them.
Medium: Astrid crosses out a larger sewing kit and leaves only needles and thread.
Medium: First Male Kin chooses laundry soap over a second food item.
Medium: Second Male Kin keeps one inexpensive packaged sweet or fruit on the list after Bjorn glances at it.
Close: Bjorn nods rather than removing it.

title: Back to the Bodega
summary: The entire household returns to the store together, and the owner recognizes them enough to treat their financial milestone as ordinary shopping rather than an event.
panelPlan: Wide: All five displaced adults enter with Carrie. The Bodega Owner recognizes the group from their first night.
Medium: Bjorn holds up the debit card.
Wide: Astrid and the two male Kin move together through the aisles choosing the specific items from the household list.
Medium: Gunnar checks prices against the tally instead of mapping the room.
Close: Carrie watches Bjorn allow other people to put things in the basket without asking permission first.

title: Prices Have Meaning
summary: The finite balance turns abstract value into household choices, but the emphasis stays on what each person chooses rather than on explaining retail systems.
panelPlan: Medium: Astrid finds needles and thread; First Male Kin lifts laundry soap; Second Male Kin adds one inexpensive snack or fruit.
Close: Gunnar looks at the total of the price tags and then at the tally paper.
Medium: Bjorn puts back one larger package of meat without ceremony.

Two-shot at the bodega counter: The owner notices Bjorn returning the larger meat package and points out a cheaper option while Astrid and the two male Kin keep their chosen practical items in the basket.
Medium: The owner shrugs and keeps ringing items.

dialogueInline.text: That one is cheaper by weight.

title: First Purchase
summary: Bjorn uses the debit card for the household's first ordinary purchase, making the account real through groceries and chosen objects rather than bank explanation.
panelPlan: Insert: Bjorn taps or inserts the debit card at the ordinary terminal.
Medium: The owner points to the PIN pad.
Close: Carrie turns away enough to give privacy.
Medium at the card reader: The approval appears; Bjorn watches the machine, then the groceries being bagged, connecting the small card to a concrete purchase.
Wide: The owner bags groceries, sewing supplies, laundry soap and the one small extra.

dialogueInline.text: Because then I can rob you.

title: Coffee Is Not Debt
summary: Bjorn's first discretionary purchase is coffee for Carrie at a neighborhood cart they can return to, separating reciprocal affection from the debt he still intends to repay.
settingText: Recurring Bushwick street coffee cart near the apartment route
panelPlan: Wide: The group stops at an ordinary street coffee cart; Astrid and the two male Kin remain together with the grocery bags.
Medium: Bjorn points to Carrie's usual order after hearing her say it once.
Medium: Bjorn pays with the debit card himself.
Two-shot at the coffee cart: Bjorn hands Carrie the large unsweetened coffee he ordered from memory, keeping it separate from the household groceries and debts.
Close on Carrie with the cup: She accepts the distinction without arguing, surprised that he remembered the order and chose to spend on it.

dialogueInline.text: One for her. Large. No sugar.
Large, no sugar is easy to remember.
Does this come out of my fifty?

title: The Things Money Became
summary: Back home, the purchases immediately become capability and the promotional toaster becomes useful, letting individual household behavior replace abstract discussion of value.
panelPlan: Wide: Groceries, sewing supplies, laundry soap and the small extra spread across the table while the toaster sits plugged in safely.
Medium: Astrid threads a needle and begins repairing the torn seam.
Medium: First Male Kin portions laundry soap while Second Male Kin opens the one small item he chose.
Medium: Gunnar lowers two pieces of bread into the toaster.
Insert at the kitchenette: The toaster pops two browned slices upward; everyone nearby looks toward the sudden mechanical motion before the ordinary smell of toast takes over.
Wide: Bjorn looks from the debit card to the repaired clothing, soap, food and toast.

title: Debt Named Properly
summary: Bjorn records Carrie's fifty beneath rent rather than trying to erase the debt immediately, turning his honor code into a household plan instead of a crisis.
panelPlan: Insert: Gunnar's tally now includes the actual grocery spend and remaining balance.
Medium: Bjorn draws a firm line beneath CARRIE 50.
Medium: Carrie drinks the coffee he bought her.
Two-shot: Bjorn taps the rent line above it.
Close: Bjorn almost objects to the word, then lets it go.

title: The Neighbor's Snack
summary: A tiny exchange with the Upstairs Neighbor turns one purchased item into relationship, continuing the building thread without making neighborhood integration a formal lesson.
panelPlan: Wide: Astrid and the two male Kin step into the hallway together to carry household trash to the proper area; the Upstairs Neighbor opens her door.
Medium: The neighbor notices the small packaged sweet in Astrid's hand.
Medium: Astrid offers one unopened piece from the household bag.
Close: The neighbor accepts and points toward the trash/recycling routine.
Wide: Bjorn watches from the doorway as the exchange happens without Carrie mediating.

dialogueInline.text: Bins are down. Recycling is blue.
Did you know where the bins were?

title: Silas Has an Angle
summary: Silas tries to turn the toaster and new account into content, but the household's ordinary use of both makes the pitch collapse before Carrie has to fight him.
panelPlan: Wide: Silas appears at the open doorway with phone half-raised while the toaster is visible on the counter.
Medium: Bjorn holds up a piece of toast.
Medium: Gunnar keeps eating and does not look at the phone.
Close: Silas lowers the device a few inches.
Medium: Carrie walks past him into the room with her coffee.

dialogueInline.text: We have eaten from it twice.
No reveal. No first reaction. Nothing.

title: The Household Ledger
summary: Gunnar expands the tally into a recurring household ledger for rent, food and obligations, making financial participation part of the group's shared life rather than Bjorn's private bank problem.
panelPlan: Wide: The household sits or stands around the table while Gunnar rewrites the tally cleanly.
Insert: Simple lines: RENT, FOOD, LAUNDRY, CARRIE 50, REMAINING.
Medium: First Male Kin points to laundry; Astrid points to food; Second Male Kin points to remaining money.
Two-shot at the evening table: Bjorn studies Gunnar's open household tally, then looks at Gunnar rather than the numbers as he realizes the record lets everyone see and alter the same plan.
Wide: The ledger stays on the table where everyone can see it.

dialogueInline.text: So we don't have to remember all of it.

title: First Toast
summary: The account's first day ends in a shared meal made from purchased groceries and a ridiculous bank toaster, with Carrie sitting inside the household rather than managing it from the edge.
panelPlan: Wide: Toast, simple food and coffee are distributed around the small room as Carrie starts the familiar motion of preparing to leave.
Medium: Astrid intercepts the departure with another piece of toast while Carrie insists that eating and staying are different things.
Group medium: Gunnar, Bjorn and Carrie continue the argument across the table; nobody physically blocks her or makes a ceremony of the invitation.
Close group beat: Carrie recognizes that the household is leaving the decision genuinely hers, which makes her resistance less convincing.
Wide: Carrie stays for another piece while the household resumes eating without declaring victory.

dialogueInline.text: That is not the same as staying.
Work will still exist after toast.
That is a dangerous thing to say around DTI.
No one is holding you here.
That is somehow making this worse.

title: What the Hoard Is For
summary: Bjorn concludes that the account matters because it can preserve obligations and support people, not because the bank convinced him recorded numbers are inherently real.
panelPlan: Insert: Debit card, bodega receipt, household ledger and brass key sit near one another on the table.
Medium: Bjorn looks at the objects, then at the room around them.
Medium: Gunnar looks at groceries, soap and repaired clothing.
Wide: Astrid and the two male Kin continue separate evening tasks.
Close: Bjorn folds the card into a safe place rather than displaying it.

dialogueInline.text: Put the card by the key.
Key opens the house. Card opens the money.
And the tally says how much.
Do you still doubt the number?

title: The Tally of Dishonor
summary: The issue closes with the unfinished household ledger visible beside everything the account enabled; Bjorn accepts that carrying a named, planned debt over time is compatible with honor.
panelPlan: Wide: Carrie stands near the door while the ledger, debit card, brass key, bodega receipt and toaster remain visible in the lived-in room.
Medium: Astrid finishes the repair she began; First Male Kin puts laundry soap away; Second Male Kin saves part of his small extra for later.
Close: Bjorn points to the CARRIE 50 line rather than crossing it out.
Medium: Gunnar leaves the tally open where everyone can see it.
Wide: After Carrie leaves, the household settles normally despite the unpaid line.
Close: Bjorn looks from the tally to the household.

dialogueInline.text: I'd be offended if I wasn't.
Then the list survives until tomorrow.

title: Next: The Skaldic Interface
summary: Editorial closing splash that turns the issue's surviving pressure toward what comes next without summarizing the issue or spoiling the next issue's payoff.
settingText: Apartment 5B table at night with newspaper, map, key and bank card
panelPlan: Full-page closing teaser at the 5B table. The key and bank card sit among practical household objects while Gunnar reads a free newspaper; Bjorn is nearby but the visual emphasis shifts from money to information.

Let the newspaper disappear into a deeper visual field of stacked print, dates and city lights without literally showing the library yet. The hook is the realization that information also lives somewhere outside the household.
Use the table surface and dark apartment negative space for integrated captions. Place 'Where does it store yesterday?' as the dominant question.
Do not show the library interior, catalog, library card, disputed history book, borrowing process, or any Issue 7 resolution.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: That is not the same as Bjorn believing in it.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: New York stores money where you cannot see it.
